feed.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions

entry.title: Quantum Landmines and Vulnerable Coin Auctions
entry.summary:
Post-quantum migration strategies are an increasingly important topic in cryptocurrency development, particularly as the threat posed by quantum computing becomes more tangible. A foundational assumption is a future scenario where quantum-safe output types exist prior to the so-called "Q-day," after which additional validation rules come into effect. These new rules require that any legacy outputs can only be spent if they are fully collateralized and if resulting outputs meet specific conditions such as time-locks or alternate spend paths. Such mechanisms bear resemblance to vault or covenant constructions, but here, implicit enforcement through soft-fork consensus changes is considered.
One innovative approach introduced is the concept of "Quantum Landmines." This involves a commit/reveal scheme enhanced by the ability to penalize theft attempts. For example, an owner like Alice might hold both legacy and quantum-safe outputs, with a trivial quantum-safe output (the landmine) secretly containing a proof-of-knowledge tied to her legacy private key. After Q-day, the spending of legacy coins requires full collateralization and adherence to new spending conditions, including time-based restrictions and proofs of pre-Q-day knowledge. Should a quantum attacker attempt to steal such funds by revealing the private key, they must wait out a designated time window before accessing the coins. Meanwhile, the legitimate owner, upon detecting a theft attempt, can reveal their proof and claim both their own coins and the attacker's collateral. This setup not only discourages attackers—who risk losing their collateral—but also obfuscates the number of genuinely vulnerable coins, thereby enhancing security through uncertainty.
However, the landmine approach faces limitations when private keys to many legacy outputs are irretrievable, allowing attackers to target these with little fear of landmine protection. To address this, the concept of a "Staked Auction" is proposed. Users can stake quantum-safe coins pre-Q-day, committing to potentially claim stolen legacy outputs by placing secret bids. Post-Q-day, if a quantum attacker spends a vulnerable output using collateral, an auction period ensues. Stakers reveal their bids, and the highest bidder claims a portion of the attacker's collateral, with the original stolen coins effectively burned. This mechanism allows for various design choices regarding bid structure, risk allocation, and collateral disposition, ensuring that as long as a landmine or lower staked bid exists, attackers cannot profit without being outbid. The system incentivizes conservative bidding from attackers and introduces strategic complexity for defenders.
Building on this, the idea of a "Sats Auction" leverages the well-known Dollar Auction game mechanics, as suggested by Neha Narula. Unlike the staked auction, it does not require pre-Q-day commitments. Every legacy coin spend initiates an open auction post-landmine timeout, where participants continue to bid to avoid becoming the second-highest bidder—who pays but recovers nothing. This dynamic can result in attackers losing all their collateral, especially if other participants escalate bidding beyond the value of the contested output. Notably, the original owner could participate in the auction and potentially recover some value, blurring the distinction between attacker and legitimate claimant. Variables such as collateral ratios, bid intervals, and the final destination of forfeited collateral are all adjustable, opening further avenues for economic experimentation.
The overarching goal of these proposals is to leverage incentives and game theory to mitigate the risk of quantum attacks on legacy coins. However, no single optimal design emerges, as priorities may differ: preventing attacks entirely, encouraging healthy staking and redistribution, or even randomizing outcomes akin to a lottery. As time progresses after Q-day, the probability increases that any spender of a vulnerable output is likely an attacker rather than the original owner, suggesting that adaptive strategies will be necessary. For further reading on the Dollar Auction concept, see the [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dollar_auction).
In conclusion, while these schemes are currently theoretical, they illustrate the potential for creative, incentive-driven defenses against quantum threats in decentralized financial systems. By combining cryptographic innovation with economic game theory, it may be possible to transform quantum vulnerability from a systemic weakness into a robust, self-policing opportunity.
